newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr savaged, yen turns on high yielders.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr savaged, yen turns on high yielders.

text.p: The Australian dollar stampeded to three month lows in frantic trade Thursday as investors scented a seachange in Japan's stance on the yen and interest rates.

Traders said investors took fright when a Japanese paper reported Eisuke Sakakibara, the Finance Ministry's forex guru, saying the yen's sharp correction was almost over. Since he was credited as the driving force behind the government's weak yen policy, the words carried huge weight.
"There's a perception the yen has turned, and panic position squaring is the result," said Citibank forex head Steve Shuster.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the local currency had crumbled to US$0.7838/43, the lowest finish since August 16, making its early US$0.7915/20 look like a distant memory.
The retreat was a bitter one for dollar bulls as they had just weathered a long-feared cut in Australian interest rates in some style, actually gaining 1/3 cent to US$0.7907/12 Wednesday.
As it was, the RBA easing proved untimely as Sakakibara went on to tell reporters this morning that he believed the Japanese economy was stronger than the market thought.
That spooked bond investors who had been driving bond prices to record highs in the belief the economy was dead in the water.

The key Japanese government bond yield leapt 11 basis points to 2.61 percent, while the main JGB futures contract lost more than a full point as the market wondered if its year-long idyll with record low interest rates might not be nearing a close.
Just a hint of that was enough to hammer high yielding currencies like the local dollar, which have benefited most from Japanese funds fleeing those painfully low rates at home.

The Australian dollar plunged to 88.05/15 yen from 90.40/50 late Wednesday, a fall of 2.6 percent and the biggest one day drop in a year. And it was in good company, with the U.S. dollar shedding nearly two big figures to 112.20 yen.
The impact was aggravated by reports U.S. ratings agency Moody's had raised concerns about the creditworthiness of some of the barrage of dual currency samurai bonds launched recently.

Around 135 billion yen worth of yen/A$ samurais were launched just last week as borrowers tapped into the seemingly inexhaustible Japanese appetite for higher yields. But now the Japanese houses that bought the bonds for retail investors were dumping in an attempt to staunch their currency losses.
"There's been a lot of talk that not all the issuers were completely creditworthy, and Moody's just added to that fear," said Michael Workman, currency economist at Commonwealth Bank.

Workman said the local dollar's decline through US$.7850 support was a bearish signal and reckoned speculators in London and New York could take advantage of the less liquid A$ market there to attack the next big bulwark at US$0.7810.
"The US$0.7810/20 area is a major chart level so speculators may feel they can trigger some sizeable stop loss sales if they get the AUD through there,' he said.

In such a case the dollar could quickly fall to US$0.7750, although he expected local exporters to be on the bid there for some much needed forex cover. Indeed, there were signs a few corporates had already been nibbling at US$0.7820.
"We've seen some good exporter interest at the lows, which makes me think the US$0.7810 level will hold intact," said Citibank Australia's Shuster.
The seismic shift in offshore markets completely dwarfed the small ripples made by today's domestic jobs data.

Employment bounced by a relatively healthy 25,500 in October afer sliding 34,100 the month before, but this was not enough to prevent the unemployment rate from rising to 8.8 percent from 8.7 percent. Analysts said the data dampened speculation the RBA would ease again soon, but did not mean a cut was out of the question in the new year. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
